explain.say: A car tyre looks like one lump of rubber, but it is built from many layers, each with its own job. The grooved tread on the outside grips the road and channels water away.

explain.say: The layers are assembled on a drum into a soft green tyre, then cooked in a mould at around 170 degrees Celsius. The heat links the rubber molecules with sulfur, called vulcanisation, and presses in the tread pattern.

faq.a: Grooves give water somewhere to go, so the rubber can still touch the road in the rain. Without them a tyre can ride up on a film of water and slide, called aquaplaning.

faq.q: Why are there steel wires inside a tyre?
faq.a: Steel belt cords under the tread stop it stretching and squirming, keeping it flat on the road for better grip, steering and longer wear. Steel wire beads lock the tyre onto the rim.
asks: What are steel belted radial tyres?

faq.q: How does a tyre hold air without a tube?
faq.a: A tubeless tyre has an inner liner made of butyl rubber, which air passes through very slowly, and its beads seal tightly against the wheel rim, so the tyre and wheel together form an airtight chamber.

Vulcanisation is heating rubber with sulfur so that sulfur atoms form bridges between its long molecules. This turns soft, sticky rubber into a tough, springy material that keeps its shape in heat and cold.
asks: Why is rubber heated with sulfur?

faq.a: Tyre rubber is mixed with carbon black, a fine soot-like powder, which makes it much stronger and more hard-wearing and protects it from sunlight. Without it, tyres would be pale and wear out quickly.
asks: What is carbon black in tyres?

facts: Charles Goodyear discovered how to vulcanise rubber with sulfur in 1839.
Carbon black is added to tyre rubber to make it stronger and longer-lasting, which is why tyres are black.
